blocks.text:
Interviewers rarely ask you to recite annotations. They ask "why" and "what happens if": why constructor injection, what happens when a transactional method calls another one on the same class, why a test passes alone and fails in a suite. This chapter collects about forty-five questions in the order interviews tend to go. Each answer is short on purpose: say it out loud in about thirty seconds, then be ready to go one level deeper. If an answer feels thin, reread the chapter named in the answer.

Answers describe Spring Boot 3.5 and the 4.x line. Where they differ, the difference is stated.

### Core Spring: IoC and dependency injection

#### 1. What is Inversion of Control, and what is dependency injection?

IoC means your code does not create and wire its own collaborators; a framework does it and calls your code. Dependency injection is the form of IoC Spring uses: a class declares what it needs (usually as constructor parameters) and the container supplies those objects. The payoff is loose coupling: you can swap a real `PaymentGateway` for a fake in a test without touching the class that uses it.

#### 2. What is a bean, and what is the ApplicationContext?

A bean is simply an object whose creation, wiring and lifecycle are managed by the Spring container. The `ApplicationContext` is that container: it reads bean definitions (from component scanning, `@Bean` methods and auto-configuration), creates the beans, injects dependencies and publishes events. `BeanFactory` is the smaller base interface; in practice you always work with an `ApplicationContext`.

#### 3. Constructor, setter or field injection: which and why?

Prefer constructor injection. It lets fields be `final`, makes required dependencies impossible to forget, works without Spring in a plain unit test (`new BookService(fakeRepo)`), and exposes circular dependencies at startup instead of hiding them. Field injection (`@Autowired` on a private field) needs reflection or the container to set up the object, so it hides how many dependencies a class has. Setter injection suits genuinely optional dependencies. A class with a single constructor needs no `@Autowired`.

#### 4. What are the stereotype annotations?

`@Component` is the generic one. `@Service`, `@Repository` and `@Controller` (and `@RestController`) are specialisations that document the layer. Technically only a few add behaviour: `@Repository` enables exception translation to Spring's `DataAccessException` hierarchy, and `@Controller` marks a web handler. `@Service` is purely semantic.

#### 5. Two beans match the type I inject. What happens?

Startup fails with `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`. Fix it with `@Primary` on the default candidate, `@Qualifier("name")` at the injection point, or by naming the parameter after the bean. If you inject `List<PaymentGateway>`, you get all of them, which is a clean way to build a strategy pattern.

#### 6. What are the bean scopes, and what is the singleton gotcha?

`singleton` (the default: one instance per container), `prototype` (a new instance each time it is requested), and the web scopes `request`, `session` and `application`. Singleton does not mean thread-safe: one instance is shared by every request thread, so a singleton service must not keep per-request state in mutable fields. Keep beans stateless, or use immutable fields. Injecting a prototype or request-scoped bean into a singleton gives you only one instance unless you inject a scoped proxy or an `ObjectProvider`.

#### 7. Describe the bean lifecycle.

Instantiate (call the constructor), populate dependencies, run `Aware` callbacks, `BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization`, then `@PostConstruct` and `afterPropertiesSet`, then `postProcessAfterInitialization` (this is where AOP proxies are usually created), then the bean is in use. On shutdown, `@PreDestroy` and `destroy` run. Prototype beans are not destroyed by the container.

#### 8. How does `@Transactional` actually work, and what is self-invocation?

Spring wraps the bean in a proxy during `postProcessAfterInitialization`. A call from outside goes through the proxy, which opens a transaction, calls the real method, then commits or rolls back. If method `a()` calls `this.b()` inside the same class, the call never touches the proxy, so `b()`'s `@Transactional` (or `@Async`, `@Cacheable`) is silently ignored. Fix by moving `b()` to another bean, or restructure so the annotated method is the entry point.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: "Why does my @Transactional method not roll back?" Three usual causes: the call came from the same class (proxy bypassed); the method is private or the class is final (cannot be proxied); or an exception was caught inside, or a checked exception was thrown (rollback happens by default only for `RuntimeException` and `Error`; use `rollbackFor` to change that). Naming all three shows you understand the proxy model.

#### 9. What does `@Configuration` with `@Bean` give you that `@Component` does not?

It is how you register objects you do not own (a third-party `ObjectMapper`, a `RestClient`) or that need construction logic. In a full `@Configuration` class, Spring proxies the class so that one `@Bean` method calling another still returns the singleton instance.

### Spring Boot and auto-configuration

#### 10. What does Spring Boot add on top of Spring?

Four things: starters (curated dependency sets with versions managed by the parent or BOM), auto-configuration (beans created for you based on the classpath and properties), an embedded server (run a jar, no WAR deployment) and production features such as Actuator. It is opinionated defaults, not a different framework.

#### 11. What does `@SpringBootApplication` do?

It is a shortcut for three annotations: `@SpringBootConfiguration` (a `@Configuration` class), `@EnableAutoConfiguration` (switch on auto-configuration) and `@ComponentScan` (scan the package of this class and below). That is why your main class must sit at the root of your package tree.

#### 12. How does auto-configuration decide what to create?

Auto-configuration classes are listed in `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` inside each starter's jar. Each class is guarded by conditions: `@ConditionalOnClass` (a library is on the classpath), `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` (back off if you defined your own), `@ConditionalOnProperty` (a switch). So if you declare a `DataSource` bean yourself, Boot's default one steps aside. Run with `--debug` to print the conditions report showing what matched and why.

#### 13. How do you override or exclude an auto-configuration?

Define your own bean of that type (the default backs off), set the relevant property, or exclude the class: `@SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)` or `spring.autoconfigure.exclude=...`.

#### 14. Where does configuration come from, and which source wins?

Properties come from many sources. From lowest to highest priority, the ones you meet daily are: defaults in code, `application.properties`/`yml` in the jar, profile-specific files (`application-prod.yml`), OS environment variables, command-line arguments (`--server.port=9090`). Higher wins. That is why a container can override a database URL with an environment variable without rebuilding the jar.

#### 15. `@Value` or `@ConfigurationProperties`?

`@Value("${app.name}")` is fine for one or two values. `@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app")` binds a whole group into a typed object (a record works well), supports relaxed binding (`APP_MAX_LOANS` maps to `app.max-loans`), nesting, validation with `@Validated`, and is easier to test. Use it for anything more than a couple of keys.

#### 16. What are profiles?

Named sets of configuration and beans, such as `dev`, `test`, `prod`. Activate with `spring.profiles.active=prod` (property, env var `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE`, or `--spring.profiles.active`). Use `application-prod.yml` for property overrides and `@Profile("dev")` to include a bean only in that profile. Never put secrets in the files that go into git; read them from the environment or a secret store.

### Spring MVC and REST

#### 17. Walk through a request in Spring MVC.

The embedded Tomcat accepts the request and hands it to the `DispatcherServlet` (the front controller). It asks `HandlerMapping` which controller method matches the URL and verb, runs interceptors, resolves arguments (`@PathVariable`, `@RequestBody` via `HttpMessageConverter`/Jackson), invokes the method, and writes the return value back as JSON. Exceptions go to `HandlerExceptionResolver`s, which is where `@RestControllerAdvice` plugs in.

#### 18. `@Controller` vs `@RestController`?

`@RestController` is `@Controller` plus `@ResponseBody`: return values are serialised straight to the response body instead of being treated as view names. For a JSON API, use `@RestController`.

#### 19. `@PathVariable`, `@RequestParam`, `@RequestBody`: when do you use each?

`@PathVariable` identifies a resource (`/books/{id}`), `@RequestParam` carries optional filters, paging and sorting (`?page=0&size=20`), and `@RequestBody` carries the JSON payload of a POST/PUT/PATCH, deserialised by Jackson. Headers use `@RequestHeader`.

#### 20. Why use DTOs instead of returning entities?

An entity mirrors your table and is managed by Hibernate; exposing it leaks columns (password hashes), couples your API to your schema, triggers lazy-loading problems during serialisation and invites mass-assignment bugs when clients send fields they should not control. A DTO, usually a `record`, is the explicit contract of the API and can change independently of the database.

#### 21. How do you validate input and report errors?

Put Bean Validation annotations (`@NotBlank`, `@Size`, `@Email`, `@Min`) on the DTO and add `@Valid` on the `@RequestBody` parameter. A failure throws `MethodArgumentNotValidException`. A `@RestControllerAdvice` with `@ExceptionHandler` methods turns it, and your own exceptions, into a consistent response. Spring supports RFC 9457 `ProblemDetail` (`application/problem+json`) for the body. Map "not found" to 404, "duplicate" to 409, "invalid but well-formed" to 422 or 400, and never return stack traces.

#### 22. PUT vs PATCH vs POST? What is idempotency?

An operation is idempotent if repeating it has the same effect as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not (two posts create two resources). PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH changes part of it (and is only idempotent if you design it that way). A client that retries after a timeout is the reason this matters.

#### 23. Which status codes do you return?

200 for success with a body, 201 plus a `Location` header on creation, 204 for success without a body (delete), 400 for malformed input, 401 not authenticated, 403 authenticated but not allowed, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 422 semantic validation failure, 500 for server bugs. The full table is in the cheat sheets.

#### 24. How do you call another HTTP service?

Use `RestClient` (Spring 6.1+, synchronous fluent API) and set connect and read timeouts, because the default is to wait too long. `RestTemplate` still works but is in maintenance mode. For reactive code there is `WebClient`. Always handle failure: a slow downstream can exhaust your threads.

#### 25. What changes with virtual threads?

Set `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` (Java 21+) and Boot runs request handling and some executors on virtual threads, so blocking calls (JDBC, `RestClient`) stop tying up scarce platform threads. It helps I/O-bound services; it does not speed up CPU-bound work, and you should still watch connection pool size.

### Data access, JPA and transactions

#### 26. JPA, Hibernate, Spring Data JPA: how do they relate?

JPA (now Jakarta Persistence) is a specification. Hibernate is the implementation Boot uses by default. Spring Data JPA sits on top: you declare an interface extending `JpaRepository<Book, Long>` and Spring generates the implementation, including derived queries such as `findByAuthorName`.

#### 27. What are the entity states?

Transient (new, not known to the persistence context), managed/persistent (tracked by the `EntityManager`; changes are flushed automatically at commit, which is called dirty checking), detached (was managed, session closed) and removed. Understanding this explains why changing a managed entity inside a transaction needs no `save()` call.

#### 28. Lazy vs eager fetching, and what is `LazyInitializationException`?

`LAZY` loads an association only when first touched; `EAGER` loads it immediately. Collections default to lazy and `@ManyToOne` defaults to eager, though lazy is usually what you want everywhere. The exception means you touched a lazy association after the session closed, typically while serialising an entity outside a transaction. Fix by fetching what you need in the query, or by mapping to a DTO inside the service.

#### 29. What is the N+1 problem and how do you fix it?

Loading N parents with one query, then lazily loading each parent's children with N more queries. It looks fine with five rows and kills you with five thousand. Fixes: `join fetch` in a JPQL query, `@EntityGraph` on the repository method, or a DTO projection that selects exactly the columns needed. Turn on `spring.jpa.show-sql` (or SQL logging) in development to see it.

#### 30. Which side owns a bidirectional relationship?

The side with the foreign key, which is the `@ManyToOne` side. The `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "author")` side is the inverse and Hibernate ignores changes made only there. Keep both sides in sync with helper methods like `author.addBook(book)`.

#### 31. How does `@Transactional` propagation work, in short?

The default is `REQUIRED`: join the caller's transaction if one exists, otherwise start one. `REQUIRES_NEW` suspends the caller's transaction and runs in a separate one that commits independently. Use `readOnly = true` for query-only methods: it signals intent and lets Hibernate skip dirty checking. Rollback is automatic for unchecked exceptions only.

#### 32. Why not `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update` in production?

Hibernate guesses schema changes, cannot rename or drop reliably, and gives no history or review. Use a migration tool (Flyway or Liquibase) with versioned SQL files and set `ddl-auto` to `validate` or `none`.

#### 33. What is open-in-view?

`spring.jpa.open-in-view` (on by default) keeps the persistence session open until the response is rendered, which hides lazy-loading errors in controllers but holds a database connection longer and encourages queries from the web layer. Many teams turn it off and fetch explicitly in the service layer.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: "Should entities implement equals and hashCode?" Be careful. Using the generated database id breaks when it is null before saving, so entities in a `HashSet` change hash code after persist. Safe options: compare on a stable business key (an ISBN), or use an id-based `equals` with a constant `hashCode`. Never include lazy collections.

### Security

#### 34. What does Spring Security do by default?

Adding the starter secures every endpoint with form login and HTTP Basic, generates a random password for a user named `user` at startup (printed in the log), and enables CSRF protection and security headers. You then define a `SecurityFilterChain` bean to describe your rules.

#### 35. Authentication vs authorisation?

Authentication answers "who are you?" (credentials checked against a `UserDetailsService` or a token validated). Authorisation answers "may you do this?" (roles and authorities checked by URL rules in the filter chain or by `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` on methods; method security needs `@EnableMethodSecurity`).

#### 36. How are passwords stored?

Never in plain text. Hash with a slow, salted algorithm through a `PasswordEncoder`; `BCryptPasswordEncoder` is the common choice, and `PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder()` stores a prefix like `{bcrypt}` so you can migrate algorithms later.

#### 37. Sessions or JWT?

Session: the server stores login state and the browser sends a cookie. Simple, easy to revoke, needs sticky sessions or a shared store when scaled. JWT: the client sends a signed token on each request, so servers stay stateless, but revocation is hard and a leaked token works until it expires. Keep tokens short-lived. In Spring you configure a resource server (`oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(...))`) rather than hand-parsing tokens.

#### 38. When can you disable CSRF?

CSRF attacks rely on the browser automatically attaching credentials such as a session cookie. A stateless API that authenticates through an `Authorization` header, with no cookies, is not exposed in that way, so disabling CSRF there is reasonable. If you use cookie-based login, keep it on.

### Testing

#### 39. What is the difference between a unit test and a Spring test?

A unit test creates the class with `new` and fakes its dependencies with Mockito: no container, runs in milliseconds. A Spring test starts some or all of the application context, so it is slower but checks wiring, JSON mapping and SQL. Aim for many unit tests and fewer slice and full-context tests (the test pyramid).

#### 40. What are test slices?

Annotations that load only part of the context. `@WebMvcTest` loads controllers, advice and filters, and you drive it with `MockMvc` while mocking the service. `@DataJpaTest` loads JPA with an embedded database and rolls back after each test. `@SpringBootTest` loads everything (with `webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT` it starts a real server).

#### 41. `@MockBean` or `@MockitoBean`?

`@MockitoBean` (Spring Framework 6.2) replaces `@MockBean`, which was deprecated in Boot 3.4 and removed in Boot 4. Use `@MockitoBean` on new code; it works in Boot 3.5 and 4.x. Import paths changed between lines, so check the import when migrating.

#### 42. How do you test against a real database?

Testcontainers starts a throwaway PostgreSQL in Docker, so tests use the same engine as production instead of H2, whose SQL dialect can differ. Boot supports `@ServiceConnection` to wire the container's URL automatically.

### Microservices basics

#### 43. Monolith or microservices?

Start with a well-structured monolith. Microservices buy independent deployment and scaling at the price of network failures, distributed data, versioning and operations work. Split when team size or scaling needs force you to, along business boundaries.

#### 44. How do services survive each other's failures?

Timeouts on every call, retries with backoff for idempotent calls only, circuit breakers (Resilience4j) to stop hammering a failing service, and fallbacks. Spring Framework 7 / Boot 4 adds core retry support; before that, Spring Retry or Resilience4j covered it.

#### 45. What does Actuator give you in production?

HTTP endpoints for health (`/actuator/health`, with liveness and readiness probes for Kubernetes), metrics through Micrometer, environment, loggers and more. Expose only what you need (`management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info`) and protect the rest; `env` and `heapdump` can leak secrets.

### How to answer well

Give the one-sentence definition first, then the reason it exists, then a trade-off or pitfall. "Constructor injection, because dependencies become explicit and final and the class is testable without Spring; the only cost is more constructor parameters, which is itself a design smell worth noticing." That structure works for almost every question here.

If you do not know, say what you would check ("I would run with `--debug` and read the conditions report") rather than guessing. Interviewers value a debugging method more than a memorised sentence.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Answer in three beats: definition, reason, trade-off or pitfall.
- The proxy model explains `@Transactional`, `@Async` and `@Cacheable` surprises, including self-invocation.
- Constructor injection, DTOs, Flyway and stateless tokens are the "right default" answers.
- Auto-configuration is conditional and backs off when you define your own bean; `--debug` shows why.
- Name a debugging step when you are unsure; it shows method.

items.question: What is wrong with this service, and why does it fail silently? `public void a() { b(); } @Transactional public` `void b() { save(); }`
items.answer: `a()` calls `b()` on `this`, bypassing the proxy, so no transaction starts. Move `b()` into another bean or annotate `a()`.

items.question: A class has two constructors and no `@Autowired`. What does Spring do?
items.answer: With several constructors and none marked `@Autowired`, Spring uses the no-argument constructor, and fails if there is none.

items.question: Which scope would you pick for a service that holds a counter of requests per user, and why is a plain singleton field wrong?
items.answer: Do not keep per-user state in the singleton; store it in a database or cache, or a thread-safe structure such as `ConcurrentHashMap`. A mutable shared field is a race condition.

items.question: Why does `ddl-auto=update` fail an architecture review?
items.answer: It changes the schema by guesswork, with no review, history or rollback. Use Flyway or Liquibase.

items.question: A controller returns an entity with a lazy collection and throws `LazyInitializationException`. Name two fixes.
items.answer: Map to a DTO inside the transactional service, or fetch the collection with `join fetch` or `@EntityGraph`.

items.question: When may CSRF be disabled?
items.answer: For stateless APIs that authenticate with a header token and use no cookies.
